content.content: The node set is the ids jj reports: a change that owns a node document is a node, and its change id — a node id is the id of the change that owns the node (D1b) — is what the set holds. The set comes from jj's change listing, scoped to the changes that own a node document (the changes touching `nodes/`, e.g. `jj log -r 'files("nodes/")'`) — never from listing the working copy's `nodes/` directory.
content.rationale: A node's id is the id of the change that owns it (D1b, xwyryumr), so the set is a set of change ids, and jj is what reports changes — the enumeration crosses the jj seam through M-jj (zruxtxrv), running its own scoped change listing rather than mapping a fixed command. Drawing the set from the read's own source keeps the two in agreement: S2-read (nqktpzuu) reads a document from the change that owns it, and a set taken from anywhere else could list nodes the read cannot reach, or miss nodes it can. A directory listing instead reads the working copy, which materialises only the nodes present at its own revision: when the working copy sits earlier in history, a node recorded later in the stack is invisible, so the set is silently partial — the same defect S2-read names for the read. A file listing at the working-copy revision (`jj file list`) answers a tree rather than the graph and inherits that same partiality. S2-path (pumpuqkv) fixes the scoping: a node is `nodes/<id>.json`, so the reported changes that touch `nodes/` are exactly the nodes, and a change that touches no node document is not one — jj's root sentinel names no file, and the empty working-copy tip owns no node.
